title: Product Revenue
watchOutFor: use `order_details.unit_price` (price at sale), not `products.unit_price` (current catalog price).
takeaway: Transactional (point-in-time) price fields differ from current catalog price fields — always aggregate historical revenue from the transaction-level price, and every non-aggregated column must appear in `GROUP BY`.
problemShort: Calculate total revenue per product, where revenue = `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)`, summed at the product level.
answerShort: 1. Join `products` to `order_details` on `product_id` to bring in line-item sales. 2. Compute per-line revenue: `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)`. 3. Aggregate (`SUM`) at product level with `GROUP BY`. 4. `ROUND` to 2 decimals for currency display. 5. Sort by `total_revenue DESC`.

title: Category Revenue
watchOutFor: `products` is the bridge — you can't join `order_details` to `categories` directly (no shared key).
takeaway: When two tables share no direct foreign key, route through the intermediate *bridge* table — and keep applying the transaction-level revenue formula at whatever grain you aggregate.
problemShort: Calculate total discounted revenue per category by rolling up product-level sales through the category hierarchy.
answerShort: 1. Start from `categories`, join to `products` on `category_id`. 2. Join `products` to `order_details` on `product_id` for transaction revenue. 3. Compute per-line discounted revenue. 4. `SUM()` grouped by category. 5. Sort by `total_revenue DESC`.

title: Top 10 Customers by Revenue
watchOutFor: `ORDER BY ... DESC` must come *before* `LIMIT`, or you get an arbitrary 10, not the top 10.
takeaway: For deterministic top-N reporting, always `ORDER BY` before `LIMIT`, and reach for window ranking when ties must be preserved.
problemShort: Identify the 10 customers with the highest total discounted revenue across all orders.
answerShort: 1. Join `customers → orders → order_details` to connect identity to transactions. 2. Compute revenue `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)`. 3. `SUM()` grouped by customer. 4. Sort by revenue descending. 5. Return top 10 with `LIMIT`.

title: Top 5 Employees by Revenue
watchOutFor: group by `employee_id` (the key), not just name — two employees could share a name and merge silently.
takeaway: Group by the stable key (`employee_id`), not display attributes — and remember `INNER JOIN` quietly drops zero-activity rows.
problemShort: Identify the 5 employees who generated the highest total discounted revenue across all orders they processed.
answerShort: 1. Join `employees → orders → order_details`. 2. Compute per-line discounted revenue. 3. `SUM()` grouped by employee. 4. Sort by revenue descending. 5. `LIMIT 5`.

title: Top 5 Customers by Number of Orders
watchOutFor: frequency (order count) ≠ value (revenue, Q03) — different business question, different list.
takeaway: Separate frequency metrics from value metrics, and use `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` defensively in joins that may later fan out to a finer grain.
problemShort: Identify the 5 customers who placed the highest number of distinct orders.
answerShort: 1. Join `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`. 2. `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` per customer. 3. Group by customer. 4. Sort by order count descending. 5. `LIMIT 5`.

title: Customers Above Average Revenue
watchOutFor: you can't write `HAVING SUM(revenue) > AVG(revenue)` — the average must be computed independently across *all* customer totals, not within one group.
takeaway: 'Above average' comparisons require two passes: aggregate per entity first, then aggregate across entities. The CTE pattern materializes that intermediate set so it can be both displayed and used in the comparison.
problemShort: Return all customers whose total revenue is strictly greater than the average total revenue computed across all customers.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`customer_revenue`) that calculates each customer's total discounted revenue. 2. In the outer query, select from that CTE. 3. Filter using a scalar subquery that computes `AVG(total_revenue)` across the entire CTE. 4. Sort by total revenue descending.

title: Employees Above Average Revenue
watchOutFor: group by `employee_id` (not name) so two employees sharing a name aren't silently merged.
takeaway: Recognize and reuse the 'CTE + scalar subquery average comparison' pattern across different entities (customers, employees) — the same structure transfers directly, only the base table and key change.
problemShort: Return all employees whose total revenue exceeds the average total revenue computed across all employees.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`employee_revenue`) that calculates each employee's total discounted revenue. 2. Select from that CTE in the outer query. 3. Filter using a scalar subquery computing `AVG(total_revenue)` over the whole CTE. 4. Sort by total revenue descending.

title: Customers Above Average Order Count
watchOutFor: 'average order count' means average *per customer*, not across orders (which would trivially be 1).
takeaway: The above-average comparison pattern applies to any aggregate — swap `SUM` for `COUNT` and it still holds. Watch how `INNER JOIN` vs `LEFT JOIN` subtly shifts the computed average.
problemShort: Return all customers whose order count exceeds the average order count computed across all customers.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`customer_orders`) that counts orders per customer. 2. Select from that CTE. 3. Filter using a scalar subquery computing `AVG(order_count)` over the whole CTE. 4. Sort by order count descending.

title: Top Categories by Number of Orders
watchOutFor: without `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)`, an order with 2+ products from the same category is counted multiple times, inflating category reach.
takeaway: Know exactly when `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` is required versus merely a safety habit — it depends on which tables are joined and at what grain, since fan-out through `order_details` can multiply an order's contribution.
problemShort: Identify the 5 categories that appear in the highest number of distinct orders.
answerShort: 1. Join `categories` to `products`, then to `order_details`, then to `orders`. 2. Count distinct `order_id` values per category using `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)`. 3. Aggregate by category. 4. Sort by order count descending and limit to the top 5.

title: Customers Purchasing from Most Categories
watchOutFor: count `DISTINCT category_id`, not `product_id` — the latter measures product variety, not category breadth.
takeaway: Distinguish 'breadth' metrics (distinct count of a dimension) from 'volume' metrics (raw counts or sums), and trace the full multi-hop join from customer to category.
problemShort: Identify the 10 customers who have purchased from the highest number of distinct product categories.
answerShort: 1. Join `customers` to `orders`, `orders` to `order_details`, and `order_details` to `products`. 2. Count distinct `category_id` values per customer using `COUNT(DISTINCT p.category_id)`. 3. Aggregate by customer. 4. Sort by category count descending and limit to the top 10.

title: Revenue by Shipper
watchOutFor: sum `order_details` revenue, not `orders.freight` — freight is the shipping cost, not the revenue handled.
takeaway: Joining through a foreign key named differently from its parent key (`ship_via` vs `shipper_id`) is routine — and always confirm whether 'revenue' means order value or shipping cost (`freight`), two metrics easy to conflate.
problemShort: Calculate the total discounted revenue of orders handled by each shipping company.
answerShort: 1. Join `shippers` to `orders` on `ship_via = shipper_id`. 2. Join `orders` to `order_details` to access transaction-level revenue. 3. Calculate discounted revenue per line item. 4. Aggregate revenue by shipper. 5. Sort by total revenue descending.

title: Employees by Unique Customers Served
watchOutFor: count `DISTINCT customer_id`, not `order_id` — the same customer can place many orders, and counting orders measures volume, not reach.
takeaway: Relationship-breadth metrics (unique customer count) answer a different question than volume/value metrics (orders, revenue) — reach for `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` whenever the question is about distinct relationships.
problemShort: Identify how many unique customers each employee has handled orders for, ranked from highest to lowest.
answerShort: 1. Join `employees` to `orders` on `employee_id`. 2. Count distinct `customer_id` values per employee. 3. Aggregate by employee. 4. Sort by unique customer count descending.

title: Products Sold Above Category Average Quantity
watchOutFor: compare each product to its *own category's* average, not the company-wide average — join `category_avg` back on `category_id`.
takeaway: Multi-level aggregation — averaging an already-aggregated per-product total up to the category grain — powers the common 'compare to peer-group average' pattern; a window function can collapse the self-join-style CTE into one clean pass.
problemShort: Find products whose total quantity sold exceeds the average quantity sold by products *within the same category* (not the company-wide average).
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`product_qty`) that sums total quantity sold per product, retaining `category_id`. 2. Build a second CTE (`category_avg`) that averages `total_qty` per category, using the first CTE as its source. 3. Join `product_qty` to `category_avg` on `category_id`. 4. watchOutFor: use `RANK()`, not `ROW_NUMBER()` — `ROW_NUMBER()` silently drops products tied for the top revenue spot.
takeaway: For 'top N per group with correct tie handling', `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` filtered on `rnk = 1` keeps every tied winner — know how `RANK`, `DENSE_RANK`, and `ROW_NUMBER` differ before choosing.
problemShort: For every category, return the product(s) generating the highest revenue within that category, including all products tied for first place.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`product_revenue`) that aggregates total discounted revenue per product, retaining `category_id`. 2. Build a second CTE (`ranked`) that applies `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY total_revenue DESC)` to rank products within each category. 3. title: Customers Above Average Orders (Correlated Subquery)
watchOutFor: `AVG(COUNT(...))` is illegal — you must average a derived table of per-customer counts, not nest aggregates directly.
takeaway: Distinguish correlated from non-correlated subqueries by whether the inner query references an outer-row column; and remember aggregates can't be nested — average a derived table of per-group counts instead.
problemShort: Return customers whose order count exceeds the average order count across all customers, computed via a subquery referenced directly inside `HAVING`.
answerShort: 1. Join `customers` to `orders` and count orders per customer. 2. In `HAVING`, compare that count against a subquery computing `AVG(order_count)`. 3. Since aggregates can't nest directly, that subquery itself wraps a derived table that first computes `COUNT(order_id) GROUP BY customer_id`. 4. Sort by order count…

title: Customers Above Average Revenue (Correlated Subquery)
watchOutFor: the revenue formula is duplicated in the outer `HAVING` and the inner subquery — keep the two copies in sync.
takeaway: A `HAVING` + subquery can replace a CTE for 'above average' filters, but it forces you to duplicate the revenue logic — a real maintainability cost that usually favors the CTE in production.
problemShort: Return customers whose total revenue exceeds the average revenue across all customers, using a `HAVING` clause referencing a subquery.
answerShort: 1. Join `customers`, `orders`, and `order_details`; aggregate discounted revenue per customer. 2. In `HAVING`, compare that total against a subquery that independently recomputes revenue per customer and averages it. 3. Sort by total revenue descending.

title: Employees Above Average Revenue (Correlated Subquery)
watchOutFor: group by `employee_id` (not name), and keep the duplicated revenue formula in sync across outer and inner queries.
takeaway: The subquery-vs-CTE 'above average' pattern transfers directly from customers to employees — group by the stable key (`employee_id`) and watch the duplicated revenue formula.
problemShort: Return employees whose total revenue exceeds the average revenue across all employees, using a `HAVING` clause referencing a subquery.
answerShort: 1. Join `employees`, `orders`, and `order_details`; aggregate discounted revenue per employee. 2. In `HAVING`, compare that total against a subquery that recomputes revenue per employee and averages it. 3. Sort by total revenue descending.

title: Customer Revenue Above Employee Average
watchOutFor: the correlation condition (`ecr2.employee_id = ecr.employee_id`) is what makes the average per-employee — drop it and it collapses to a single global average.
takeaway: A correlated subquery references an outer-row column and re-evaluates per row — here it yields a per-employee average; pre-aggregate into a CTE first to keep it cheap and readable.
problemShort: For each employee, return the customers whose revenue (from orders handled by that employee) exceeds the average revenue of all customers handled by that same employee.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`employee_customer_revenue`) that aggregates revenue per employee-customer pair. 2. In the outer query, select from that CTE. 3. Filter using a correlated subquery that computes `AVG(revenue)` for *only the rows matching the current row's `employee_id`*. 4. Sort by employee and then by revenue…

title: Customers Above Average Revenue Using CTE
watchOutFor: the comma-join to `overall_avg` is only safe because that CTE returns exactly one row — a stray `GROUP BY` there would silently multiply result rows.
takeaway: Compose multiple CTEs so one holds detail-level results and another holds a single benchmark; an implicit cross join (`FROM a, b`) safely broadcasts a one-row scalar across every detail row.
problemShort: Use a CTE to calculate per-customer revenue, and a second CTE to calculate the overall average, then return customers exceeding that average.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`customer_revenue`) for per-customer discounted revenue. 2. Build a second CTE (`overall_avg`) that computes a single scalar: the average of `total_revenue` across the first CTE. 3. In the final SELECT, combine both CTEs (the second produces one row, broadcast across the first) and filter where…

title: Top 5 Customers by Revenue Using CTE
watchOutFor: the CTE is pure style here — don't assume it's faster; and `ORDER BY` must precede `LIMIT` or you get an arbitrary 5.
takeaway: CTEs are primarily a readability/composability tool rather than a performance optimization for simple single-use cases — this is the foundational pattern the more advanced CTE questions (Q21–Q24) build on.
problemShort: Use a CTE to calculate per-customer revenue, then return the top 5 customers by revenue from that CTE.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`customer_revenue`) that aggregates discounted revenue per customer. 2. Select all columns from the CTE. 3. Sort by total revenue descending. 4. Limit to the top 5 rows.

title: Employees Above Average Revenue Using Multiple CTEs
watchOutFor: `JOIN ... ON >` is only safe because the average CTE is single-row — against a multi-row CTE it becomes a non-equi join that explodes result rows.
takeaway: `JOIN ... ON` accepts arbitrary boolean conditions, not just equality — useful for 'compare to benchmark' queries, but only safe when the right-hand side's cardinality (here, one row) is guaranteed.
problemShort: Calculate employee revenue in one CTE, average revenue in a second CTE, and join them using the comparison itself as the join condition.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`employee_revenue`) for per-employee discounted revenue. 2. Build a second CTE (`avg_revenue`) producing the single average revenue value across all employees. 3. Join the two CTEs using `ON er.total_revenue > ar.avg_rev` as the join condition itself. 4. Sort by total revenue descending.

title: Top Employee by Revenue Using 3 CTEs
watchOutFor: `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` silently drops ties — compare to `MAX()` so every tied top employee is returned.
takeaway: For 'top 1 with ties', compare against `MAX()` (not `LIMIT 1`) so every tied row surfaces; chain CTEs each with one clear responsibility — aggregate, reduce, filter.
problemShort: Find the employee(s) with the single highest total revenue, using a layered three-CTE structure: aggregate, find the maximum, then filter to matches.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`employee_revenue`) aggregating discounted revenue per employee. 2. Build a second CTE (`max_revenue`) computing the single highest revenue value across all employees. 3. Build a third CTE (`ranked_employees`) joining the first two on equality (`total_revenue = max_rev`), which naturally includes…

title: Best Customer per Employee
watchOutFor: use `RANK()` not `ROW_NUMBER()` (keeps ties), and never omit `PARTITION BY employee_id` or you rank customers globally instead of per employee.
takeaway: The 'best X per Y' pattern is a partitioned window ranking: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Y ORDER BY metric DESC)` then filter `rnk = 1` — `RANK()` preserves ties, and presentation joins belong after the windowing step.
problemShort: For every employee, return the customer (or customers, if tied) generating the highest revenue from orders that employee handled.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`employee_customer_revenue`) aggregating revenue per employee-customer pair. 2. Build a second CTE (`ranked`) applying `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY total_revenue DESC)`. 3. Filter to `rnk = 1`, returning every customer tied for the top spot per employee. 4. Join in `employees` and…

title: Highest Revenue Product per Category (CTE + Window Function)
watchOutFor: use `RANK()` (not `ROW_NUMBER()`) and keep `PARTITION BY category_id`; the `categories` join is presentation-only and must not alter the ranking.
takeaway: The 'top N per group with ties' window pattern transfers across entities; adding descriptive columns from a dimension table after the ranking step improves readability without changing the analytical result.
problemShort: For every category, return the product(s) generating the highest revenue within that category, including all ties.
answerShort: 1. Build a CTE (`product_revenue`) aggregating discounted revenue per product, retaining `category_id`. 2. Build a second CTE (`ranked`) applying `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY total_revenue DESC)`. 3. Join the ranked result to `categories` to bring in `category_name`. 4. Filter to `rnk = 1` to keep…

title: Customers and Order Count
watchOutFor: use `COUNT(o.order_id)`, not `COUNT(*)` — `COUNT(*)` counts the NULL-padded row and reports 1 instead of 0 for no-order customers.
takeaway: Before choosing `INNER` vs `LEFT JOIN`, ask "should rows with no match still appear?" — and when counting over a `LEFT JOIN`, always count the joined column (`COUNT(o.order_id)`), never `COUNT(*)`.
problemShort: Return every customer and their total order count, ensuring customers with zero orders still appear in the result with a count of 0, rather than being excluded.
answerShort: 1. Start from `customers` and LEFT JOIN to `orders` on `customer_id`, preserving every customer regardless of order history. 2. Aggregate using `COUNT(o.order_id)` — counting the joined column, not `COUNT(*)`, so unmatched customers correctly show 0. 3. Group by customer. 4. Sort by order count descending.

title: Customers and Latest Order Date
watchOutFor: in `DESC` sorts PostgreSQL puts `NULL` first — add `NULLS LAST` or never-ordered customers float to the top of a 'most recent' report.
takeaway: Most aggregates (except `COUNT`) ignore and propagate `NULL` correctly on their own — so `MAX` over an all-NULL group gives the right `NULL` answer — but you must manage `NULL` sort position explicitly with `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST`.
problemShort: Return every customer along with the date of their most recent order, showing `NULL` for customers who have never placed an order.
answerShort: 1. Start from `customers` and LEFT JOIN to `orders` on `customer_id`. 2. Aggregate using `MAX(o.order_date)`, which naturally returns `NULL` for customers with no matching orders. 3. Group by customer. 4. Sort descending by latest order date, explicitly placing `NULL` values (never-ordered customers) last.

title: Products and Total Quantity Sold
watchOutFor: `SUM()` over an all-NULL group returns `NULL`, not `0` — wrap in `COALESCE(..., 0)` when the business asks to "display 0".
takeaway: Know the difference between "NULL is the correct answer" (Q26) and "NULL must be converted to a business default" (here) — `COALESCE` is the standard tool for supplying a zero default over a `LEFT JOIN` + `SUM` aggregate.
problemShort: Return every product and the total quantity sold across all orders, displaying 0 for products that have never appeared in any order.
answerShort: 1. Start from `products` and LEFT JOIN to `order_details` on `product_id`. 2. Aggregate using `SUM(od.quantity)`, wrapped in `COALESCE(..., 0)` to convert the `NULL` result (from products with no matching `order_details` rows) into a literal 0. 3. Group by product. 4. Sort by total quantity sold descending.

title: Customers with No Orders
watchOutFor: avoid `NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` — a single `NULL` in the subquery makes it return an empty result set entirely.
takeaway: Master the anti-join pattern (`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE key IS NULL`, or its `NOT EXISTS` equivalent) for "find rows with no match" — and remember `NOT IN` is unsafe whenever the subquery column can contain `NULL`.
problemShort: Return only the customers who have zero orders on record — no aggregation or counts needed, just the filtered list itself.
answerShort: 1. LEFT JOIN `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`, preserving every customer regardless of order history. 2. Filter to rows where `o.order_id IS NULL`, which identifies customers with no matching order at all. 3. (Alternative shown: `NOT EXISTS`, often more efficient and equally NULL-safe.)

title: Products Never Ordered
watchOutFor: same `NOT IN` NULL trap as Q28 — use the anti-join (`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE od.order_id IS NULL`) or `NOT EXISTS`.
takeaway: The anti-join pattern is about the *pattern*, not the tables — once internalized on customers (Q28), it transfers directly to products, or any "entity with no matching child row" question.
problemShort: Return only the products that have never appeared in any order, with no aggregation needed — just the filtered list of products themselves.
answerShort: 1. LEFT JOIN `products` to `order_details` on `product_id`, preserving every product regardless of sales history. 2. Filter to rows where `od.order_id IS NULL`, which identifies products with no matching order line item at all. 3. (Alternative shown: `NOT EXISTS`, an equally valid and often more efficient approach.)

title: Products Never Ordered (Join-Key Filter)
watchOutFor: filter on a *right-hand* table column (`od.product_id IS NULL`) — `p.product_id IS NULL` can never be true for an existing product row.
takeaway: Any column from the right-hand table works in the `IS NULL` filter because an unmatched `LEFT JOIN` row has *every* right-side column set to `NULL` — just never filter on a left-side column, which can never be `NULL` for a real row.
problemShort: Return only the products that have never appeared in any order, with no aggregation needed — just the filtered list of products themselves.
answerShort: 1. LEFT JOIN `products` to `order_details` on `product_id`, preserving every product regardless of whether it has been ordered. 2. Filter to rows where `od.product_id IS NULL`, which identifies products with no matching row in `order_details` at all — using the join key itself, which mirrors the `ON` condition…

takeaway: In a chained `LEFT JOIN`, every link must stay `LEFT` or no-match rows vanish downstream; `SUM()` returns `NULL` (not `0`) for empty groups, so `COALESCE` is always the fix when a zero default is required.

takeaway: `COUNT(order_id)`, `COUNT(customer_id)`, and `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` look similar but answer different business questions — pick the one that matches the grain (unique relationships here), and group on the primary key even when only a derived display name is shown.

answerShort: 1. Start from `employees` and LEFT JOIN to `orders` on `employee_id`, preserving every employee regardless of order history. 2. title: Latest Order Per Customer
watchOutFor: ROW_NUMBER needs a deterministic tie-breaker (order_id) or the 'latest' row can change between runs.
takeaway: Top-1-per-group = `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC, unique_id)` in a CTE, then filter `rn = 1` outside.
problemShort: For every customer who has ordered, return exactly one row describing their latest order (latest `order_date`; if two orders share a date, the higher `order_id` wins).
answerShort: 1. Number each customer's orders with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC)`. 2. Keep only `rn = 1` in the outer query (window results cannot be filtered in the same `WHERE`). 3. Join `customers` for the company name and sort by `customer_id`.

title: Rank Vs Dense Rank Product Prices
watchOutFor: RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK does not (1,1,2). Know which the question wants.
takeaway: RANK skips numbers after ties, DENSE_RANK does not, ROW_NUMBER never ties. Pick based on how the question treats equal values.
problemShort: For each product, show its price rank within its category using both `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` (highest price = 1).
answerShort: 1. Join `products` to `categories`. 2. Compute `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` over the same window: `PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY unit_price DESC`. 3. Sort by category, rank, then `product_id` as the tie-breaker.

title: Top 3 Products By Revenue Per Category
watchOutFor: Aggregate revenue first, then rank; you cannot filter on the rank in the same SELECT that computes it.
takeaway: Top-N per group: aggregate, rank with `PARTITION BY`, then filter the rank in an outer query.
problemShort: For each category, return the top 3 revenue positions (using `DENSE_RANK`), where revenue = `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)` from `order_details`.
answerShort: 1. CTE `product_revenue`: sum net revenue per product (with its `category_id`). 2. CTE `ranked`: `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY revenue DESC)`. 3. Filter `revenue_rank <= 3`, join `categories` for the name, and round.

title: Running Total Of Monthly Revenue
watchOutFor: Aggregate to one row per month first; then SUM() OVER (ORDER BY month) gives the cumulative total.
takeaway: Running total = `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY t ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` over pre-aggregated rows.
problemShort: Return one row per order month with its revenue and the running total of revenue to date.
answerShort: 1. CTE `monthly`: `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` and sum net revenue per month. 2. Outer query: `SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`. 3. Round both values and order by month.

title: Three Month Moving Average Revenue
watchOutFor: The first two rows have partial windows; show months_in_window so the reader knows the average is not over 3 months.
takeaway: Moving averages use a bounded frame: `AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY t ROWS BETWEEN n-1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.
problemShort: Return each order month's revenue, the number of months in its trailing window, and the 3-month trailing moving average.
answerShort: 1. CTE `monthly`: revenue per `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`. 2. Define `WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY order_month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`. 3. Compute `AVG(revenue) OVER w` and `COUNT(*) OVER w`; round and order by month.

title: Month Over Month Revenue Change
watchOutFor: The first month has no previous month, so LAG returns NULL; guard the division with NULLIF.
takeaway: `LAG()` compares a row with its predecessor without a self-join; guard percentage math with `NULLIF`.
problemShort: For each order month, return revenue, previous month revenue (via `LAG`), absolute change, and percent change rounded to 2 dp.
answerShort: 1. CTE `monthly`: revenue per month. 2. CTE `with_prev`: add `LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_month)`. 3. Compute change and `100.0 * change / NULLIF(prev, 0)`; round and order by month.

title: Days Until Next Customer Order
watchOutFor: Partition by customer, or LEAD will read another customer's order.
takeaway: `LEAD()` with `PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY time` gives 'next event' metrics per entity in one pass.
problemShort: For each order, return the same customer's next order ID, its date, and the number of days between the two (NULL if there is no next order).
answerShort: 1. Define `WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id)`. 2. Use `LEAD(order_id)` and `LEAD(order_date)` over `w`. 3. Subtract `order_date` from the lead date to get days (date − date = integer). 4. Order by customer, date, order_id.

title: Customer Share Of Total Revenue
watchOutFor: An empty OVER () spans the whole result set, so the grand total is available on every row without a subquery.
takeaway: `SUM(x) OVER ()` puts the grand total on every row, making percent-of-total a one-step calculation.
problemShort: For each customer, return their net revenue, the company-wide total, and their share as a percentage (2 dp), largest first.
answerShort: 1. CTE `customer_revenue`: net revenue per customer. 2. Outer query: `SUM(revenue) OVER ()` gives the grand total on every row. 3. Share = `100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER ()`; round and order by share descending, then `customer_id`.

title: Customer Revenue Quartiles
watchOutFor: NTILE splits by row count, not by value; tied revenues can land in different quartiles.
takeaway: `NTILE(n)` makes n equal-count buckets over an ordered set — always add a tie-breaker.
problemShort: Assign every customer to a revenue quartile (1 = highest revenue) using `NTILE(4)`.
answerShort: 1. CTE `customer_revenue`: net revenue per customer. 2. `NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id)` to bucket customers. 3. Join `customers`; order by quartile, revenue descending, `customer_id`.

title: Employee Revenue Percentile Rank
watchOutFor: PERCENT_RANK = (rank − 1)/(n − 1) starts at 0; CUME_DIST = rows ≤ current / n never reaches 0.
takeaway: `PERCENT_RANK` = relative rank from 0 to 1; `CUME_DIST` = share of rows at or below — know both formulas.

answerShort: 1. CTE `employee_revenue`: net revenue per employee. 2. Compute `PERCENT_RANK()` and `CUME_DIST()` over `ORDER BY revenue` (ascending, so higher = better). 3. Join employees, round, order by revenue descending then `employee_id`.

title: Average Gap Between Employee Orders
watchOutFor: Compute LAG before aggregating — window functions cannot be nested inside AVG().
takeaway: Compute row-level window values (LAG) in one CTE, aggregate in the next — window functions cannot be nested in aggregates.
problemShort: For each employee, compute the number of orders, the average and maximum days between consecutive orders, and the difference between their average gap and the average of all employees' averages.
answerShort: 1. CTE `order_gaps`: `order_date - LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id)`. 2. CTE `employee_gaps`: per employee `COUNT(*)`, `AVG(gap_days)`, `MAX(gap_days)`. 3. Outer query: `avg_gap_days - AVG(avg_gap_days) OVER ()`; join employees; order by `avg_gap_days`, `employee_id`.

title: Orders Per Year And Month
watchOutFor: group by both year AND month — grouping by month alone merges January 1996 with January 1997.
takeaway: Period reports group on every part of the period key — year AND month — and cast `EXTRACT` to int for clean output.
problemShort: Return the number of orders placed per calendar year and month, with year and month as integers.
answerShort: 1. Extract the year and month from `order_date` with `EXTRACT(...)::int`. 2. Group by both parts and `COUNT(*)` the orders. 3. Order by year, then month.

title: Revenue By Quarter
watchOutFor: after joining to order_details, count orders with COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), not COUNT(*), or you count line items.
takeaway: Quarterly revenue = join to line items, group by year + `EXTRACT(QUARTER)`, `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)`, and cast to numeric before rounding.
problemShort: Return order count and net revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) per year and quarter.
answerShort: 1. Join `orders` to `order_details` on `order_id`. 2. Extract year and quarter from `order_date`. 3. `SUM` the net line revenue and `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)`. 4. Round revenue with `ROUND(...::numeric, 2)` and order by year, quarter.

title: Late Shipments With Days Late
watchOutFor: DATE - DATE returns an integer number of days in PostgreSQL; unshipped orders (NULL shipped_date) are neither late nor on time.
takeaway: In PostgreSQL, `date - date` is an integer day count — the simplest way to measure lateness, after filtering out NULL ship dates.
problemShort: Return all shipped orders where shipped_date > required_date, with the number of days late.
answerShort: 1. Keep only orders with a non-NULL `shipped_date`. 2. Filter `shipped_date > required_date`. 3. Compute `shipped_date - required_date` as `days_late`. 4. Sort by `days_late DESC`, then `order_id`.

title: Average Days To Ship Per Shipper
watchOutFor: exclude unshipped orders explicitly; and AVG of integers must be cast to numeric before ROUND(..., 2).
takeaway: Lead-time metrics = `date - date` aggregated per group, with the NULL population excluded once in WHERE so every metric shares the same base.
problemShort: Per shipper, return shipped order count, average and maximum days between order_date and shipped_date.
answerShort: 1. Join `shippers` to `orders` on `ship_via = shipper_id`. 2. Filter `shipped_date IS NOT NULL`. 3. Aggregate `COUNT`, `AVG` and `MAX` of `shipped_date - order_date`. 4. Round the average and sort fastest first, tie-break on `shipper_id`.

title: Unshipped Orders Older Than 30 Days
watchOutFor: use the fixed reference DATE '1998-12-31' as 'today' — never CURRENT_DATE — and test shipped_date with IS NULL, not = NULL.
takeaway: Aging reports need a fixed as-of date, `IS NULL` for open items, and `as_of - date` for integer days open.
problemShort: Return unshipped orders with order_date more than 30 days before 1998-12-31, with days open and an overdue flag.
answerShort: 1. Filter `shipped_date IS NULL`. 2. Keep rows where `order_date < DATE '1998-12-31' - 30`. 3. Compute `days_open` and a boolean `past_required_date`. 4. Sort oldest first (`days_open DESC`), tie-break on `order_id`.

title: Employee Age At Hire And Tenure
watchOutFor: AGE(later, earlier) — argument order matters; and dividing day counts by 365 drifts on leap years, so use AGE for completed years.
takeaway: Use `AGE(later, earlier)` + `EXTRACT(YEAR ...)` for completed years and plain `date - date` for exact days.
problemShort: Return each employee's age at hire, tenure in completed years and tenure in days as of 1998-12-31.
answerShort: 1. `AGE(hire_date, birth_date)` gives an interval in years/months/days; extract YEAR for completed years. 2. `AGE(DATE '1998-12-31', hire_date)` for tenure years. 3. `DATE '1998-12-31' - hire_date` for tenure in days. 4. Sort youngest hire first, tie-break on `employee_id`.

title: Orders By Day Of Week
watchOutFor: TO_CHAR(..., 'Day') pads names to 9 characters and sorts alphabetically — sort by a numeric day number instead.
takeaway: Group weekdays by a numeric `ISODOW` key for correct ordering, and display a trimmed `TO_CHAR` name alongside it.
problemShort: Return order count and net revenue for each day of the week, ordered Monday through Sunday.
answerShort: 1. Join `orders` to `order_details`. 2. Derive `EXTRACT(ISODOW ...)::int` and `TRIM(TO_CHAR(order_date, 'Day'))`. 3. Group by both; count distinct orders and sum net revenue. 4. Order by `day_number`.

title: Year Over Year Revenue Growth
watchOutFor: compute growth from unrounded totals and guard the divisor with NULLIF; the first year has no prior year, so its growth is NULL.
takeaway: Aggregate to one row per period, then `LAG` over the period order; compute growth on unrounded values with `NULLIF` on the divisor.
problemShort: Return yearly net revenue, previous year's revenue and YoY growth % (all rounded to 2 decimals).
answerShort: 1. CTE `yearly`: sum net revenue per `EXTRACT(YEAR ...)::int`. 2. Use `LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_year)` for the prior year. 3. Growth % = `(revenue - prev) * 100.0 / NULLIF(prev, 0)`. 4. Round each output column and order by year.

title: Customers Inactive In Last Six Months
watchOutFor: customers with no orders at all must be included — use LEFT JOIN and keep last_order_date IS NULL explicitly.
takeaway: Churn = aggregate to each customer's latest order via LEFT JOIN, then filter on that max — and keep the NULL never-ordered rows explicitly.
problemShort: Return customers whose most recent order is before 1998-06-30, or who have no orders, with last order date and days since then.
answerShort: 1. CTE: LEFT JOIN customers to orders; take `MAX(order_date)` and `COUNT(o.order_id)` per customer. 2. Cutoff = `(DATE '1998-12-31' - INTERVAL '6 months')::date` = 1998-06-30. 3. Keep rows where last order is NULL or before the cutoff. 4. Order by `last_order_date NULLS FIRST`, tie-break on `customer_id`.

title: First Order Month Cohort Size
watchOutFor: a customer's cohort is the month of their FIRST order — take MIN per customer before counting, or repeat customers are counted in several cohorts.
takeaway: Cohorts start with one row per customer — `DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date))` — then count and window over those rows.
problemShort: Return, per first-order year and month, the number of newly acquired customers and the cumulative total.
answerShort: 1. CTE `first_orders`: per customer, `DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date))::date`. 2. Group by cohort month and `COUNT(*)` customers. 3. Running total with `SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (ORDER BY cohort_month)`. 4. Split into integer year and month; order by both.

title: Employee Full Name And Initials
watchOutFor: `||` returns NULL if any operand is NULL; `CONCAT()` treats NULL as an empty string.
takeaway: `||` for NOT NULL inputs, `CONCAT`/`CONCAT_WS` when NULLs are possible; `LEFT`, `UPPER` and `LOWER` handle simple formatting.
problemShort: For every employee, return the full name (`first_name last_name`), upper-case initials, and the last name in lower case.
answerShort: 1. Concatenate `first_name || ' ' || last_name` for the full name. 2. Take `LEFT(..., 1)` of each name, concatenate and wrap in `UPPER()`. 3. Apply `LOWER(last_name)` and order by `employee_id`.

title: Customers Matching Name Patterns
watchOutFor: `LIKE` is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL; use `ILIKE` (or `LOWER()`) for case-insensitive matches.
takeaway: Anchor with `%` to choose starts-with vs contains, and reach for `ILIKE` whenever letter case should not matter.
problemShort: Return customers whose `company_name` starts with `La` (case-sensitive) or contains `market` (case-insensitive).
answerShort: 1. Filter with `company_name LIKE 'La%'` OR `company_name ILIKE '%market%'`. 2. Label the matching rule with a `CASE` expression. 3. Order by `customer_id`.

title: Longest Product Names
watchOutFor: Ties on length are common, so add a unique tie-breaker after `name_length DESC`.
takeaway: `LENGTH` counts characters; always pair a computed sort key with a unique tie-breaker before `LIMIT`.
problemShort: Return the 10 products with the longest `product_name`, with the character count.
answerShort: 1. Compute `LENGTH(product_name)`. 2. Sort by length descending, then `product_id` to break ties. 3. Keep the first 10 rows with `LIMIT`.

title: Split Contact Name Into First And Last
watchOutFor: Names can have more than two words; `SPLIT_PART(name, ' ', 2)` drops everything after the second word.
takeaway: `SPLIT_PART` for a fixed field, `POSITION` + `SUBSTRING` for "everything after the first delimiter".
problemShort: For customers in Germany, split `contact_name` into `first_name` and `last_name` and show the position of the first space.
answerShort: 1. Find the first space with `POSITION(' ' IN contact_name)`. 2. `SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 1)` gives the first word. 3. `SUBSTRING(contact_name FROM space_pos + 1)` keeps the rest, including multi-word surnames. 4. Filter to Germany and order by `customer_id`.

title: Normalize Postal Codes With Replace
watchOutFor: `REPLACE` is literal and case-sensitive; nest calls to strip several different characters.
takeaway: `REPLACE` for literal substitutions (nest for several), `REGEXP_REPLACE ... 'g'` or `TRANSLATE` for character sets.
problemShort: For customers whose `postal_code` contains a space or a hyphen, return the original code, a cleaned upper-case code with spaces and hyphens removed, and both lengths.
answerShort: 1. Keep rows where `postal_code ~ '[ -]'`. 2. Nest `REPLACE(REPLACE(postal_code, ' ', ''), '-', '')` and wrap in `UPPER`. 3. Compare lengths before and after, ordered by `customer_id`.

title: Product List Per Category With String Agg
watchOutFor: Without `ORDER BY` inside `STRING_AGG`, the list order is not guaranteed.
takeaway: `STRING_AGG(col, sep ORDER BY col)` turns a group into a sorted delimited list — sort inside the aggregate.
problemShort: For each category, return the number of non-discontinued products and an alphabetical comma-separated list of their names.
answerShort: 1. Join `categories` to `products` and keep `discontinued = false`. 2. Group by category. 3. `STRING_AGG(product_name, ', ' ORDER BY product_name)` builds the list; `COUNT(*)` counts. 4. Order by `category_name`.

title: Parse Category Description Keywords
watchOutFor: The last item in Northwind descriptions is joined with `and`, so a plain comma count is one short.
takeaway: Count delimiters with `LENGTH - LENGTH(REPLACE())`, pick fields with `SPLIT_PART` (negative index from the end) and clean with `TRIM`/anchored regex.
problemShort: For each category, return the first keyword of the description (text before the first comma), the number of comma-separated items, and the final item with any leading `and ` removed.
answerShort: 1. `SPLIT_PART(description, ',', 1)` gives the first keyword. 2. Count commas with `LENGTH(description) - LENGTH(REPLACE(description, ',', ''))`, then add 1. 3. Take the last comma field with `SPLIT_PART(description, ',', -1)`, `TRIM` it and strip a leading `and ` with `REGEXP_REPLACE`. 4. Order by `category_id`.

title: Customer Cities Per Country With Distinct String Agg
watchOutFor: With `DISTINCT` inside `STRING_AGG`, the inner `ORDER BY` must use the same expression being aggregated.
takeaway: `STRING_AGG(DISTINCT x, sep ORDER BY x)` deduplicates a list; filter groups with `HAVING` and tie-break the outer sort.
problemShort: For countries with 5 or more customers, return a 3-letter upper-case country code, the country, the customer count, the distinct city count, and the distinct cities as a ` | `-separated alphabetical list.
answerShort: 1. Group customers by `country`. 2. `COUNT(*)` customers and `COUNT(DISTINCT city)` cities. 3. `STRING_AGG(DISTINCT city, ' | ' ORDER BY city)` for the list. 4. `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5`; order by customer count descending, then country.

title: Product Price Bands
watchOutFor: `CASE` returns the first matching `WHEN`, so order the bounds from low to high (or high to low) consistently.
takeaway: Order `CASE` branches so each bound only needs one comparison; first match wins.
problemShort: Return each product with its price and price band.
answerShort: 1. Write a searched `CASE` with `WHEN unit_price < 20`, then `< 50`, then `ELSE`. 2. Order by `product_id`.

title: Product Count And Average Price Per Band
watchOutFor: Group by the same CASE expression (or its alias / ordinal), not by `unit_price`.
takeaway: Bucket with `CASE`, group by the bucket, then aggregate — the CASE becomes the grouping key.
problemShort: For each price band (Budget < 20, Mid-range < 50, Premium), return the product count, min, max and average price.
answerShort: 1. Compute the band with `CASE`. 2. `GROUP BY` the band alias. 3. Aggregate `COUNT`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `AVG`. 4. Order by `min_price` so bands appear cheapest first.

title: Employee Shipping Status Counts
watchOutFor: `shipped_date > required_date` is NULL for unshipped orders, so check `IS NULL` first.
takeaway: Conditional aggregation = one GROUP BY, many `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)` / `SUM(CASE ...)` columns.
problemShort: For each employee, count total orders, on-time shipments, late shipments (shipped after the required date) and unshipped orders.
answerShort: 1. Join employees to orders. 2. Use `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)` for on-time and late. 3. Use `SUM(CASE WHEN shipped_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` for unshipped (to show both styles). 4. Group by employee and order by `employee_id`.

title: Pivot Category Revenue By Year
watchOutFor: A FILTER with no matching rows returns NULL, not 0 — wrap in `COALESCE` for a clean pivot.
takeaway: Pivot = `GROUP BY` the row key + one `SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE col = value)` per output column.
problemShort: Return net revenue per category for 1996, 1997 and 1998 as separate columns, plus a total column, each rounded to 2 dp.
answerShort: 1. Join categories → products → order_details → orders. 2. For each year, `SUM(net) FILTER (WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = yyyy)`. 3. `COALESCE(..., 0)` and round each column. 4. Group by category and order by `category_name`.

title: Custom Country Sort Order With CASE
watchOutFor: The CASE gives the priority group only; you still need secondary keys for a deterministic order.
takeaway: Custom sort = `ORDER BY CASE ... END` for the priority, then real columns down to a unique key.
problemShort: Return customers in USA, Canada, Mexico, Brazil and Argentina ordered by a custom priority (USA, then Canada/Mexico, then others), then by country and company name.
answerShort: 1. Filter to the five Americas countries. 2. Map country to a priority number with `CASE`. 3. Order by the priority, then `country`, then `company_name`, then `customer_id`.

title: Average Order Value With NULLIF And COALESCE
watchOutFor: Dividing by a zero order count raises an error; `NULLIF(count, 0)` turns it into NULL instead.
takeaway: `NULLIF(divisor, 0)` makes division safe; `COALESCE(agg, 0)` turns missing aggregates into zero — use each where its meaning fits.
problemShort: For all customers in Germany, return order count, total net revenue (0 if none) and average order value (NULL if no orders), plus a status label.
answerShort: 1. `LEFT JOIN` customers to orders and order_details so customers without orders stay. 2. `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)` and `SUM` net revenue. 3. `COALESCE(SUM(...), 0)` for revenue; `SUM(...) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT ...), 0)` for the average. 4. Label with `CASE` and order by `customer_id`.

title: Customer Value Segment Summary
watchOutFor: Customers with no orders have NULL revenue; COALESCE before bucketing or they fall into the wrong segment.
takeaway: Segment in a CTE (one row per entity, NULLs coalesced), aggregate per segment, and order segments with a `CASE`.
problemShort: Segment all customers by total net revenue and return per segment: customer count, total revenue, average revenue per customer and share of total revenue (%), ordered High, Medium, Low, Inactive.
answerShort: 1. CTE `cust_rev`: LEFT JOIN customers to orders/order_details and `COALESCE(SUM(...), 0)` per customer. 2. CTE `seg`: bucket revenue with `CASE` (Inactive when 0). 3. Group by segment; compute share with `SUM(SUM(revenue)) OVER ()`. 4. Order with a `CASE` mapping segments to 1–4.

title: Insert New Shipper With Returning
watchOutFor: Do not supply `shipper_id`; let the `SERIAL` default assign it and read it back with `RETURNING`.
takeaway: Insert without the id, read generated values with `RETURNING`, and wrap in a CTE when you need ordered output.
problemShort: Insert shippers `Speedy Freight` (phone `(503) 555-0101`) and `Polar Logistics` (phone `(503) 555-0102`) and return the new rows. Runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, so the data change is undone after grading.
answerShort: 1. `INSERT INTO shippers (company_name, phone) VALUES (...), (...)` — omit the id. 2. Add `RETURNING shipper_id, company_name, phone`. 3. Wrap in a CTE and `SELECT ... ORDER BY shipper_id` so the output order is guaranteed.

title: Raise Prices For One Supplier
watchOutFor: An `UPDATE` without `WHERE` changes every row in the table.
takeaway: `UPDATE ... SET col = f(col) WHERE ... RETURNING` — always scope with `WHERE` and verify with `RETURNING`.
problemShort: Increase `unit_price` by 5% (rounded to 2 dp) for products of `supplier_id = 1`, and return product id, name and new price. Runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, so the data change is undone after grading.
answerShort: 1. `UPDATE products SET unit_price = ROUND(unit_price * 1.05, 2)`. 2. Restrict with `WHERE supplier_id = 1`. 3. `RETURNING` the new price; wrap in a CTE and order by `product_id`.

title: Update Prices Using A Join With FROM
watchOutFor: In `UPDATE ... FROM`, the join condition goes in `WHERE`; missing it updates every product once per category row.
takeaway: `UPDATE target SET ... FROM other WHERE join_condition AND filter` — never list the target in `FROM` again.
problemShort: Increase `unit_price` by 10% (2 dp) for every product in the `Seafood` category, and return the product, category name, and new price. Runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, so the data change is undone after grading.
answerShort: 1. `UPDATE products p SET ... FROM categories c`. 2. `WHERE c.category_id = p.category_id AND c.category_name = 'Seafood'`. 3. `RETURNING` columns from both tables; wrap in a CTE and order by `product_id`.

title: Delete Small Order Lines With Returning
watchOutFor: `RETURNING` output is unordered and only lists rows; aggregate it in an outer query to summarise the deletion.
takeaway: `WITH d AS (DELETE ... RETURNING ...) SELECT ... FROM d` lets you audit, summarise or archive exactly what was removed.
problemShort: Delete `order_details` rows with `quantity <= 2` and return each deleted line with its net value. Runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, so the data change is undone after grading.
answerShort: 1. `DELETE FROM order_details WHERE quantity <= 2 RETURNING *` inside a CTE. 2. Compute the line value in the outer `SELECT`. 3. Order by the primary key `(order_id, product_id)`.

title: Upsert Customers With On Conflict
watchOutFor: `ON CONFLICT` needs a unique index or constraint on the conflict columns; `EXCLUDED` refers to the proposed row.
takeaway: Upsert = `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col`, backed by a unique index.
problemShort: Upsert `ALFKI` (new city `Hamburg`, postal code `20095`) and a new customer `ZZTOP` (`ZZ Top Traders`, contact `Billy Gibbons`, `Houston`, `77002`, `USA`). Return each row and whether it was inserted or updated. Runs…
answerShort: 1. `INSERT INTO customers (...) VALUES (...), (...)`. 2. `ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE SET city = EXCLUDED.city, postal_code = EXCLUDED.postal_code`. 3. `RETURNING ..., CASE WHEN xmax = 0 THEN 'inserted' ELSE 'updated' END`. 4. Wrap in a CTE and order by `customer_id`.

title: Create Order And Lines With Chained CTE Inserts
watchOutFor: Sub-statements in one `WITH` cannot see each other's changes in the table — pass data between them through `RETURNING`.
takeaway: Chain inserts with CTEs and pass generated keys through `RETURNING` — one atomic statement for header and lines.
problemShort: In one statement, insert the order header, insert its two lines using the new `order_id` and current product prices, and return the lines with their totals. Runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, so the data change is undone…
answerShort: 1. CTE `new_order`: `INSERT INTO orders ... RETURNING order_id`. 2. CTE `lines`: `INSERT INTO order_details SELECT new_order.order_id, p.product_id, p.unit_price, v.qty, 0 FROM new_order CROSS JOIN (VALUES ...) v JOIN products p ... RETURNING *`. 3. Final `SELECT` joins `lines` to `products` for names and orders by…

title: Create Customer Revenue Summary Table As Select
watchOutFor: `CREATE TABLE AS` copies data and column types only — no primary key, indexes or defaults.
takeaway: CTAS snapshots a query into a table; add keys afterwards, and remember it never refreshes on its own.
problemShort: Create `customer_revenue_summary` from an aggregate query, add a primary key on `customer_id`, and return the top 10 customers by revenue from the new table. Runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, so the data change is undone…
answerShort: 1. `CREATE TABLE customer_revenue_summary AS SELECT ... GROUP BY customer_id`. 2. `ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY (customer_id)`. 3. `SELECT` from the new table ordered by `revenue DESC, customer_id` with `LIMIT 10`.

title: Add Column And Check Constraint To Products
watchOutFor: Adding a `NOT NULL` constraint fails if existing rows are NULL — backfill first, then set the constraint.
takeaway: Add column → backfill → enforce (`NOT NULL`, `CHECK`) — constraints are validated against existing rows when added.
problemShort: Add a `price_band` column, backfill it with `CASE`, make it `NOT NULL` with a `CHECK` on the allowed values, add a `CHECK (unit_price >= 0)` constraint, and return the product count per band. Runs inside `BEGIN ……
answerShort: 1. `ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN price_band VARCHAR(10)`. 2. `UPDATE products SET price_band = CASE ... END` to backfill. 3. `ALTER COLUMN price_band SET NOT NULL` and add `CHECK (price_band IN (...))` and `CHECK (unit_price >= 0)`. 4. `SELECT` count and min price per band ordered by `min_price`.

title: Categories With A Wide Price Spread
watchOutFor: Aggregate conditions belong in HAVING; WHERE runs before rows are grouped.
takeaway: Conditions on groups go in HAVING, and several aggregate conditions can be combined there with AND.
problemShort: List categories that contain at least one product under 10 and at least one product over 40, with the product count, cheapest and dearest price and the average price (2 dp), widest spread first.
answerShort: 1. Join products to categories and group by category. 2. Keep groups where MIN(unit_price) < 10 AND MAX(unit_price) > 40 (HAVING). 3. Order by the spread MAX − MIN, descending, then by name.

title: Countries With Repeat Customers
watchOutFor: Count orders per customer first, then count customers per country: one GROUP BY can't do both.
takeaway: When a metric aggregates an aggregate, compute the inner level in a CTE and aggregate it again.
problemShort: For each country, count customers who ordered at all, how many of them ordered at least twice, and the repeat share in percent (1 dp). Only list countries with at least one repeat customer, highest share first.
answerShort: 1. CTE: orders per customer (customer_id, country, COUNT). 2. Outer query: group the CTE by country. 3. COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE order_count >= 2) gives repeat customers; HAVING keeps countries with at least one.

title: Customers Whose Every Order Shipped On Time
watchOutFor: 'Every order is on time' means 'no order is late or unshipped' — test the opposite with NOT EXISTS.
takeaway: 'For every row' is written as 'there is no row that breaks the rule': NOT EXISTS.
problemShort: List customers with at least one order where none of their orders is unshipped or shipped after its required date, with their number of orders, most orders first.
answerShort: 1. Join customers to their orders and group, so customers without orders drop out. 2. WHERE NOT EXISTS (an order of this customer that is unshipped OR shipped later than required). 3. Order by order count, then customer_id.

title: Product Names With Three Or More Words
watchOutFor: Split on '\s+' (one or more whitespace characters), not ' ', or double spaces create empty words.
takeaway: REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_ARRAY plus UNNEST turns text into words you can count, sort and filter with normal SQL.
problemShort: For each product whose name has at least three words, show the word count and its longest word (ties broken alphabetically), most words first.
answerShort: 1. REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_ARRAY(TRIM(product_name), '\s+') gives the words as an array. 2. ARRAY_LENGTH(..., 1) counts them; keep names with 3 or more. 3. A scalar subquery UNNESTs the array and picks the longest word.

title: Revenue By Discount Tier
watchOutFor: discount is a REAL: 0.05 is stored as 0.0500000007, so `discount <= 0.05` is false. Use half-open ranges.
takeaway: Bucket with half-open ranges, especially on floating-point columns; boundaries with = are fragile.
problemShort: Bucket order lines into No discount, Under 10%, 10% to under 15%, and 15% or more; show lines, units, net revenue (2 dp) and average quantity (1 dp) per tier, in tier order.
answerShort: 1. CASE with half-open ranges: = 0, < 0.1, < 0.15, else. 2. GROUP BY 1 groups by the CASE expression. 3. Number the labels so ORDER BY discount_tier sorts them in tier order.

title: Employee Reporting Chain With A Recursive CTE
watchOutFor: The anchor selects the top of the tree (reports_to IS NULL); the recursive part joins children to rows already found.
takeaway: WITH RECURSIVE walks a hierarchy: anchor at the root, then repeatedly join children to the rows found so far.
problemShort: Return every employee with their depth below the top manager (0 for the top) and the full path of names from the top, sorted so each manager is followed by their team.
answerShort: 1. Anchor: employees with no manager, depth 0, path = their name. 2. Recursive member: join employees to the previous level on reports_to, depth + 1, path || ' > ' || name. 3. Order by path so the tree reads top-down.

title: Selling Periods From Order Dates (Gaps And Islands)
concepts: Running SUM as a group id
watchOutFor: Flag the first row of each island (gap > 7 days), then a running SUM of the flags numbers the islands.
takeaway: Gaps and islands: flag where a new island starts, running-SUM the flags into an island id, then aggregate by it.
problemShort: Group order dates into periods in which consecutive order dates are at most 7 days apart. For each period show its number, start date, end date, orders and revenue (2 dp), in date order.
answerShort: 1. Aggregate to one row per order date (orders, revenue). 2. Flag a new period when the gap to the previous date (LAG) is over 7 days or there is no previous date. 3. Running SUM of the flags gives each row its period number; group by it.

title: Customers Making Up 80% Of Revenue (Pareto)
watchOutFor: Order the running total by revenue AND customer_id with a ROWS frame, or tied revenues are summed together.
takeaway: Cumulative shares need a running SUM with an explicit ROWS frame and a unique ORDER BY.
problemShort: List the smallest set of top customers whose combined revenue reaches 80% of all revenue, with each customer's revenue (2 dp) and the cumulative share in percent (1 dp), largest first.
answerShort: 1. CTE: net revenue per customer. 2. Running SUM ordered by revenue DESC, customer_id with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW; total with SUM() OVER (). 3. Keep customers whose running total before them is still under 80% of the total.

title: Customer Buying Episodes (Sessionization)
watchOutFor: A new episode starts on a customer's first order or after a gap of more than 60 days.
takeaway: Sessionize with LAG for the gap, a flag for 'new session', and a running SUM of flags as the session id.
problemShort: For each customer with at least two orders, count their buying episodes, their orders, and the days between their first and last order; most episodes first.
answerShort: 1. LAG(order_date) per customer gives the gap to their previous order. 2. Flag 1 when the gap is NULL (first order) or over 60 days; a running SUM per customer numbers the episodes. 3. Group by customer: COUNT(DISTINCT episode), COUNT(*), MAX − MIN date.

title: Each Customer's Favourite Product With LATERAL
watchOutFor: LATERAL lets the subquery refer to c.customer_id; CROSS JOIN drops customers with no orders.
takeaway: LATERAL is a per-row subquery in FROM: the cleanest way to write top-N per group.
problemShort: For every customer who has ordered, show the product they bought the most units of (ties broken by product name) and the units, highest first.
answerShort: 1. FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (subquery). 2. The subquery sums units per product for c.customer_id, orders by units DESC, product_name, LIMIT 1. 3. Order the result by units, then customer_id.

title: Second Highest Price Per Category Without Window Functions
watchOutFor: 'Exactly one distinct price above it' means second highest; COUNT(DISTINCT) handles ties.
takeaway: Nth highest without windows: count the distinct higher values with a correlated subquery.
problemShort: For each category, list the product(s) priced at the second-highest distinct price, with the price, by category and product name.
answerShort: 1. For each product, count the distinct prices in its category that are higher than its own. 2. Keep products where that count is exactly 1. 3. Join categories for the name and order by category, product.

title: Month-End Open Order Backlog
watchOutFor: An order is open at a month end if it was placed by then and not yet shipped by then (or never shipped).
takeaway: Point-in-time questions join a calendar to rows that were 'active' on each date.
problemShort: For each month end in 1997, count orders that were open at that date and their average age in days (1 dp, 0 when none), in date order.
answerShort: 1. GENERATE_SERIES over the 12 months, converted to month-end dates. 2. LEFT JOIN orders where order_date <= month_end AND (shipped_date IS NULL OR shipped_date > month_end). 3. Count orders and average month_end − order_date per month end.

title: Products Shipped To Germany And The USA But Not France
watchOutFor: INTERSECT binds tighter than EXCEPT, so A INTERSECT B EXCEPT C is (A ∩ B) − C.
takeaway: INTERSECT and EXCEPT say 'both' and 'but not'; INTERSECT runs first unless you add parentheses.
problemShort: List products that appear on orders shipped to Germany and on orders shipped to the USA, but never on orders shipped to France, by product id.
answerShort: 1. Three SELECTs of product_id from order lines filtered by ship_country. 2. Combine: Germany INTERSECT USA EXCEPT France. 3. Use the combined set in WHERE product_id IN (...).

title: Median And 90th Percentile Order Value Per Employee
watchOutFor: PERCENTILE_CONT needs WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …) and returns double precision; cast to numeric before ROUND(…, 2).
takeaway: Use PERCENTILE_CONT … WITHIN GROUP for medians and percentiles, over the right grain (orders, not lines).
problemShort: For each employee, compute their order count, mean, median and 90th-percentile net order value (all 2 dp), highest median first.
answerShort: 1. CTE: net value per order (order_id, employee_id). 2. Group by employee: AVG, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) and PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY order_value). 3. Join employees for names; order by median.

title: Product Pairs Frequently Bought Together
watchOutFor: Join order lines of the same order with b.product_id > a.product_id so each pair appears once.
takeaway: Self-join on the shared key with a < b to generate each pair once, then count.
problemShort: List product pairs that appear together in two or more orders, with both names and the number of shared orders, most frequent first.
answerShort: 1. Self-join order_details a and b on the same order_id with b.product_id > a.product_id. 2. Join products twice for the names. 3. Group by the pair and keep pairs with COUNT(*) >= 2.

title: Suppliers With No Orders Since June 1998 (NOT EXISTS vs NOT IN)
watchOutFor: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a NULL; NOT EXISTS has no such trap and plans as an anti-join.
takeaway: Prefer NOT EXISTS for 'has no matching row': NULL-safe and planned as an anti-join.
problemShort: List suppliers none of whose products appear on an order dated on or after 1998-06-01, by supplier id.
answerShort: 1. For each supplier, look for any order line of their products with order_date >= '1998-06-01'. 2. Keep suppliers where that search finds nothing (NOT EXISTS). 3. Order by supplier_id.

title: Weekly Revenue For Q1 1997 With A Sargable Filter
watchOutFor: Filter with order_date >= '1997-01-01' AND < '1997-04-01', not EXTRACT(...) on the column, so an index can be used.
takeaway: Filter dates with a half-open range on the bare column (sargable), and fill calendar gaps with GENERATE_SERIES.
problemShort: Show net revenue (2 dp, 0 for weeks without orders) for every Monday-starting week overlapping Q1 1997, from the week of 1996-12-30 to the week of 1997-03-24.
answerShort: 1. GENERATE_SERIES produces every Monday from 1996-12-30 to 1997-03-24. 2. A CTE sums revenue per DATE_TRUNC('week', order_date) for orders in [1997-01-01, 1997-04-01). 3. LEFT JOIN the weeks to the totals and COALESCE missing weeks to 0.
